div.p: Glioblastoma (GBM) is a lethal brain tumor with few therapies. Targeting Chitinase 3-like 1 (CHI3L1), we used our SpaceDock structure-based virtual screen of 377 billion compounds, synthesized 60 top hits, and validated nine binders. Lead compound 9e (K d = 19.11 μM) reduced viability and STAT3 signaling in 3D GBM spheroids. These findings demonstrate the potential of reactivity-aware ultralarge screening to identify modulators of nonenzymatic, dynamic targets in complex cancer models.

div.head: ■ INTRODUCTION
div.p: Glioblastoma (GBM) is an aggressive and notoriously hard-totreat brain cancer. 1 Its diffuse spread, cellular heterogeneity, and dynamic tumor microenvironment 2 limit the effectiveness of surgery, radiation, and chemotherapy. 3 In the United States, GBM causes over 10,000 deaths annually, 4 with median survival of 12-18 months; ∼25% survive beyond one year, and few reach five years. 5 GBM reprograms immune cells, particularly macrophages, to support rather than attack the tumor, driving angiogenesis, immune suppression, and faster progression. 6 This immunosuppressive reprogramming also limits current immunotherapies, underscoring the need for new targets to reverse it. 7 Even with the use of approved drugs like Temozolomide, 8 bevacizumab, 9 and tumor-treating fields, 10 mutations in the IDH1 11 or EGFR genes 12 efforts to treat GBM remain largely unsuccessful. Key barriers include treatment resistance, poor drug penetration across the blood-brain barrier, and an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. 13 These challenges underscore the need for new small molecules and improved screening strategies.

Among the potential molecular targets receiving growing attention is Chitinase-3-like protein 1 (CHI3L1). 14 This protein is secreted by cells 15 and, although it shares structural similarities with active enzymes called chitinases, it lacks the key residues needed for enzymatic function. 16 Instead, it plays a significant role in processes like inflammation, 17 tissue remodeling, 18 and cancer progression. 19 In the case of GBM, CHI3L1 levels are often elevated, and the protein appears to help steer macrophages toward a state that supports tumor growth, promotes new blood vessel formation, and suppresses immune responses. 20 Through these connections, CHI3L1 influences multiple signaling cascades in tumor biology and immune evasion, notably activating the STAT3 pathway, a driver of immunosuppression in GBM. 20 The pursuit of selective small-molecule inhibitors targeting CHI3L1 has remained limited. [21][22][23] CHI3L1 is challenging to drug because it lacks enzymatic activity and stable receptorligand interactions, instead acting as a flexible, contextdependent signaling regulator that transiently engages receptors such as IL-13Rα2, RAGE (receptor for advanced glycation end products), and VEGFR2 (Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor Receptor 2). 24 We present one of the largest virtual screening approaches ever described, leveraging the efficiency of our recently described SpaceDock virtual screening method, 25 to search in a chemical space of 377 billion synthetically feasible molecules for CHI3L1 inhibitors. Of 45 synthesized candidates, three were validated by multiple orthogonal assays as promising leads for optimization.

div.head: ■ RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
div.p: Structure-Based Screening Of A Virtual Chemical Space of 377 Billion Compounds. We applied an in-house structure-driven, reaction-aware ligand design strategy (Space-Dock) 25 tailored to the unique demands of nonenzymatic, structurally flexible proteins such as CHI3L1. Moving beyond reliance on extensive preassembled virtual libraries, our approach initiates from commercially available building blocks, which are docked onto experimentally or computationally characterized protein surfaces of interest. (Figure 1).

Reagent docking poses (20 per building block) are then systematically scanned for one of 40 possible organic chemistry S1), depending on strict topological (distances, angles, torsional angles) relationships and organic chemistry cross-compatibility. Upon successful linkage (covalent bond formation, ring closure), newly enumerated SpaceDock ligands are energy minimized in the target active site and redocked to ascertain that the same pose can be recovered again. Quality check of remaining poses 26 eliminated dubious solutions (high strain energy, too many unsatisfied hydrogen-bonds and ionic bonds at the protein-ligand interface) which are then submitted to two independent and rigorous physics-based absolute binding free energy estimates (Hyde 27 and VM2 28 ) to keep only best scorers. Clustering by maximum common substructures afforded 60 clusters out of which the best VM2 scorer was purchased for synthesis at Enamine (Kyiv, Ukraine). Out of the 60 virtual hits, 45 could indeed be synthesized at sufficient purity (>90% by LC-MS).

div.p: Primary Screening by MST. Virtual hits were tested at the single concentration of 250 μM for binding to a fluorescentlabeled His-tagged hCHI3L1 protein. Based on the normalized fluorescence (Fnorm) values (Figure 2A), 15 potential hits (1c, 1d, 1e, 2a, 2d, 2e, 3a, 3b, 4a, 4c, 6a, 7d, 8a, 8b, 9e) were identified. Comparison of compound fluorescence with a blank/ reference (CHI3L1 labeled and treated with 2.5% DMSO instead of a test compound) identified eight compounds (2d, 2e, 3a, 3b, 4c, 6a, 8b, and 9e) that exhibited higher or lower fluorescence than the blank (Figure 2B). To eliminate false positives due to signal interference or fluorophore interactions, additional control experiments were performed on those eight hits, including autofluorescence screening (Figure 2C) and a quenching assay (Figure 2D).

In the autofluorescence assay, compounds 2e, 3b, 4c, 6a and 8b exhibited high intrinsic fluorescence at the detection wavelength, whereas the fluorescence signals for compounds 2d, 3a, and 9e remained within acceptable limits for MST analysis. In the quenching assay, compounds 2d, 2e, 3b, and 4c showed concentration-dependent quenching effects and were therefore excluded from further analysis.

Based on these criteria, compounds showing minimal signal interference across all assays were considered suitable for MST analysis. Through this refinement process, nine compounds� 1c, 1d, 1e, 2a, 3a, 4a, 7d, 8a, and 9e�were confirmed as valid hits with reliable binding profiles.

Dose-Response Confirmation. The potential hits identified from the single-dose screening were further evaluated in a dose-dependent MST assay to confirm their direct binding affinity for CHI3L1 (Figure 3). Among the nine candidates, three compounds 3a, 4a, and 9e exhibited a clear dosedependent response, indicating these are likely true binders.

Interestingly, none of the three hits were available in the catalogue of 20 million commercially available screening compounds directly purchasable at E-molecule (https://www. emolecules.com/products/screening-compounds), thereby confirming the value of screening much larger "on-demand" chemical spaces.

Hit confirmation by SPR. To support the MST results, we evaluated binding affinities of compounds 3a, 4a, and 9e using SPR. Compound 3a S1A) did not exhibit a dosedependent response, while compound 4a (Figure S1B) showed a high relative response indicative of nonspecific binding. However, compound 9e showed a clear, dose-dependent binding response, yielding a dissociation constant (K d ) of 19.11 μM (Figure S1C). The SPR sensorgram for compound 9e is presented in Figure S2. Notably, the dose-dependent activity of 9e observed in both SPR and MST assays closely mirrors the behavior of the positive control compound G28 (Figure S3). Importantly, 9e exhibits a K d of 19.11 μM, which represents an improvement over G28 (K d = 51.42 μM).

Given the low molecular weight of compound 9e (MW = 277.75) and an estimated logP of 2.31 (ACD/ChemSketch v2010), it presents an excellent ligand efficiency 29 of 0.35 kcal mol -1 and a valuable start for hit to lead optimization. According to SpaceDock, the compound is hydrogen-bonded to two central polar residues (D207, Y206) and exhibit aromatic interactions to F261 and Y352. Distal aromatic groups (chloroindane, oxadiazole) fit into the two apolar ends of the pocket (Figure S4). However, the pocket remains empty at the vicinity of E290 and M204/M350, suggesting that adequate substitutions to reach both amino acids may improve the hit potency.

AlphaLISA-Based Assessment of Compounds Targeting hCHI3LA-Galectin-3 Interaction. To investigate the ability of selected compounds to inhibit the interaction between hCHI3L1 and Galectin-3, compounds 3a, 4a, and 9e were evaluated using an AlphaLISA-based inhibition assay (Figure 4A). The assay was performed in technical triplicates under optimized conditions. Compound 3a exhibited no detectable inhibition, while compound 4a showed a modest inhibition of 13.23%. Compound 9e displayed the highest level of inhibition among the three, at 20.87%. These results suggest that 4a and 9e may weakly interfere with the hCHI3L1-Galectin-3 interaction, highlighting them as potential starting points for further optimization.

Evaluation of the Therapeutic Potential Using GBM Organoids. To evaluate the functional impact of compound 9e in a biologically relevant context, we utilized a 3D multicellular GBM spheroid model comprising GBM cells, endothelial cells, and macrophages. Treatment with compound 9e led to a pronounced, dose-dependent decrease in spheroid viability, achieving statistical significance at concentrations as low as 25 μM (Figure 4B). This outcome aligns with the respective CHI3L1 binding affinity of compound 9e. Although the IC 50 of compound 9e in GBM spheroids (62.4 ± 7.8 μM) is within the range expected for an early hit (Figure S5), structural analysis revealed additional unoccupied regions in the predicted binding pocket (Figure S4) that are amenable to substitution, supporting 9e as a suitable starting point for lead-optimization.

To further validate the CHI3L1 dependency of 9e, we performed a phenocopy experiment using a CHI3L1-neutralizing antibody (Figure S6). Treatment with the antibody reduced spheroid viability to a similar extent as 9e (76% vs 71% of control), and cotreatment of antibody and 9e did not produce an additive effect (73%). This lack of additivity demonstrates that 9e and the antibody act through the same pathway, supporting CHI3L1-dependent activity of 9e.

To further probe target engagement, we quantified pSTAT3 levels in GBM spheroids using a HTRF assay. Compound 9e elicited a dose-dependent reduction in pSTAT3 (Figure 4C). Collectively, these findings support compound 9e as an inhibitor of the CHI3L1-STAT3 axis, capable of impairing tumor spheroid viability and dampening downstream signaling in a relevant 3D coculture system. To directly contextualize 9e against the known CHI3L1 tool compound G28, both compounds were evaluated side-by-side in 3D GBM spheroids (Figure 4B,C). Although G28 revealed more potent reduction in spheroid viability than 9e, only compound 9e resulted in a significant reduction of phospho-STAT3 levels (Figure 4C). This uncoupling between the effect of G28 on viability and its lack of STAT3 inhibition suggests that G28 may not act through the CHI3L1-STAT3 signaling axis in this model. In contrast, 9e reduces both spheroid viability and STAT3 phosphorylation (Figure 4B,C), consistent with a CHI3L1-dependent mechanism of action.

div.head: ■ CONCLUSION
div.p: This study applies a structure-guided, reaction-aware virtual screening (SpaceDock) of 377 billion compounds to identify CHI3L1 inhibitors, a conformationally dynamic GBM target. Prioritized candidates yielded lead 9e, which showed micromolar affinity, blocked CHI3L1-Galectin-3 interaction, and reduced viability and STAT3 signaling in 3D GBM organoids. These results position 9e as a promising lead and highlight SpaceDock as a versatile platform for targeting elusive proteins through integrated computational design, biophysical screening, and tumor-relevant validation.

figure.head: Figure 1 .
figure.figDesc: Figure 1. Structure-based organic-chemistry driven ligand design. (A) Three-dimensional structure of CHI3L1 bound to a small molecule inhibitor (PDB 8R4X). Key protein-ligand hydrogen bonds are displayed by magenta dots. (B) Generative design workflow yielding 60 synthesizable hits. At each step, several filters are introduced to restrain the generative design. We here ensured that the two key hydrogen bonds to Y216 and D217 are conserved throughout the workflow. Number of solutions are indicated, at each step, in the bottom diagram.

figure.head: Figure 2 .
figure.figDesc: Figure 2. (A) Primary screening of molecules from at 250 μM (with 2.5% DMSO). The blue, green, black, and purple indicates the potential hits, negative control/reference (buffer with 2.5% DMSO), nonbinder, positive control (G28); 22 (B) Comparison of initial fluorescence of compounds with reference having labeled hCHI3L1 with 2.5% DMSO. The red dots indicate the compounds that may have signal interference or fluorophore interactions; (C) Autofluorescence and (D) quench test of candidates from single-dosage screening. Dotted lines in (C) and (D) indicate the threshold values (mean negative control ± 3 × SD) used to flag compounds with excessive autofluorescence or quenching.

figure.head: Figure 3 .
figure.figDesc: Figure 3. MST-based confirmation of CHI3L1 binding by compound 3a, 4a and 9e, respectively. The graph displays dose-dependent changes in normalized fluorescence (Fnorm [%]) plotted against increasing concentrations of each ligand. Data are mean ± SD (n = 3).
